The **Mississauga Transitway** is a [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) system in [Mississauga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississauga "Mississauga"), [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada. It comprises a series of purpose-constructed [bus-only roadways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_lane "Bus lane"), as well as reserved lanes on existing city streets and portions of [Highway 403](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_403 "Ontario Highway 403"), that together form a continuous 18 km (11 mi) route spanning most of the city from [Winston Churchill Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill_Boulevard "Winston Churchill Boulevard") in the west to the junction of Highways [401](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_401 "Ontario Highway 401") and [427](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_427 "Ontario Highway 427") in the east on the border with [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"). Service on the Transitway is provided by [MiWay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiWay "MiWay") and [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit "GO Transit"), with some stations providing connections to [Brampton Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brampton_Transit "Brampton Transit") and [Toronto Transit Commission (TTC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Transit_Commission "Toronto Transit Commission") bus services.

Originally proposed in the 1970s, the Mississauga Transit plan has evolved over time. A minimum of eighteen studies were made between 1970 and 1992. In the 1990s, a serious proposal intended to build a "transitway" from Ridgeway Drive at the very western edge of the city;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-TransitToronto-1) this was eventually revised to its current state, with construction beginning in November 2010.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN101119-3) The first stretch of the present Transitway opened between [Hurontario Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurontario_Street "Hurontario Street") and [Dixie Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Dixie_Road "List of roads in Mississauga") on November 17, 2014.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-CBC_Opening-4) Other remaining sections faced delays, and were open in stages until the eastern terminus, [Renforth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renforth_station "Renforth station"), was opened on November 22, 2017.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN140506-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-GO-Transitway-6) There were plans to eventually extend Transitway service to a new regional bus terminal at the [Kipling subway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipling_station "Kipling station") in southern Etobicoke,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-7) which came to fruition with the opening of [the terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipling_station#MiWay_Bus_Terminal "Kipling station") on January 4, 2021.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-9)

## Design and operation

The Mississauga Transitway consists of two busways and bus-priority lanes. The western busway segment parallels [Highway 403](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_403 "Ontario Highway 403") from the western terminus at Winston Churchill Boulevard to [Erin Mills Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Erin_Mills_Parkway "List of roads in Mississauga"). From there, buses use dedicated shoulder lanes on Highway 403 and Centre View Drive to reach MiWay's [City Centre Transit Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississauga_City_Centre_Transit_Terminal "Mississauga City Centre Transit Terminal") on [Rathburn Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Rathburn_Road "List of roads in Mississauga"). The longer eastern busway begins east of Hurontario Street, paralleling Highway 403 to [Cawthra Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Cawthra_Road "List of roads in Mississauga") and then following Eastgate Parkway on its north and west side to [Eglinton Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eglinton_Avenue "Eglinton Avenue"), and Eglinton on its north side to the eastern terminus at Renforth Drive at the boundary with Toronto.

Bus services along the Mississauga Transitway operate similarly to that of the [Ottawa Transitway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Transitway "Ottawa Transitway") network, using a mixture of express and local routes that call at intermediate stations constructed along the route. Because the Transitway does not directly connect to any major transit hubs other than the City Centre Terminal, all routes that use the Transitway travel in mixed traffic to reach other outlying termini such as [Kipling subway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipling_station "Kipling station").

The Transitway is shared by MiWay standard and [articulated buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articulated_bus "Articulated bus") for intra-city travel, along with [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit_bus_services "GO Transit bus services")-operated [highway coaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach_(bus) "Coach (bus)") and [double-decker buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-decker_bus "Double-decker bus") along inter-city routes. The busways have a maximum speed of 80 km/h (50 mph) on the dedicated roadway between stations, and 50 km/h (31 mph) in the vicinity of stations. MiWay buses operating along the Transitway stop at all stations [by request](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_stop "Request stop"), while GO Transit routes only make stops at Winston Churchill, Erin Mills, Dixie, and Renforth stations (depending on the route).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-TransitToronto-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-Rapid1-10)

### Funding and construction

The Transitway project, estimated to cost [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_dollar "Canadian dollar")259 million,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN101119-3) was funded as part of the Government of Ontario's [MoveOntario 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MoveOntario_2020 "MoveOntario 2020") plan, with both the federal and provincial governments contributing up to a total of $173 million.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-11) Construction responsibilities were divided between [Metrolinx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrolinx "Metrolinx") and the City of Mississauga: Metrolinx was responsible for the western segment between Winston Churchill and Erin Mills, a portion of the eastern segment between Hurontario and Cawthra, and Renforth Station; while the city was responsible for all other stations and segments.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-GO-Transitway-6) Construction on the eastern segment began in November 2010,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN101119-3) while Metrolinx launched construction of the western segment in November 2013.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-12)

Including construction, land, design and bus acquisition, Mississauga’s cost was at least $328 million. Metrolinx 's cost was over $200 million. The federal government contributed $83 million, bringing the total to approximately $611 million.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-13)

### MiWay

With the opening of the first phase on November 17, 2014, MiWay adjusted three of its routes to use the eastern section of the corridor, with service initially operating Monday to Saturday from 4:30 AM to 10:30 PM. A fourth route, 110 University, began using the Transitway lanes on Highway 403 on September 7, 2015 with the opening of Erin Mills station, which is the only Transitway station served by this route.

On January 8, 2017, with the opening of the new Winston Churchill station, new Sunday service was implemented on 109 Meadowvale Express, expanding service along the full length of the Mississauga Transitway to 7 days a week.

## Stations

Access to the stations along the BRT portion of the route is by means of [pedestrian walkways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidewalk "Sidewalk"), with Kiss & Ride areas at most stations and [Park & Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_and_ride "Park and ride") lots at selected stations. All stations are wheelchair-accessible ([![Image 75: Disabled access](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Wheelchair_symbol.svg/20px-Wheelchair_symbol.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility "Disabled access")), have heated [waiting areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_shelter "Bus shelter"), and similar to the [Züm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCm "Züm") service operated by [Brampton Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brampton_Transit "Brampton Transit"), loading platforms designed for [level boarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_boarding "Level boarding").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-14) Transitway stations are unstaffed and there are no faregates or [fare-paid areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paid_area "Paid area") within them. Fare payment is done upon boarding buses as with on-street routes.

A multi-modal interchange with the western extension of the [TTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Transit_Commission "Toronto Transit Commission")'s [Line 5 Eglinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_5_Eglinton "Line 5 Eglinton") is currently under construction at Renforth station.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-22) A later phase will terminate at the nearby [Pearson International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Pearson_International_Airport "Toronto Pearson International Airport"). Originally proposed in 2007 under the city of Toronto's [Transit City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_City "Transit City") plan, the first phase of Line 5 will open as far west as [Mount Dennis station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Dennis_station "Mount Dennis station") at [Weston Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weston_Road "Weston Road") in 2023. The Renforth interchange would open later, pending the financing for the project,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-TheStar-2016-11-02-23) and would feature a full-service below grade BRT station, but only an at-grade median surface stop for the LRT, requiring transferring passengers to cross Commerce Boulevard and descend a set of stairs to access the BRT.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-24)

As of 2020 however, in an addendum to the Line 5 extension, the addendum showed the future Renforth LRT station partially at-grade and the station located off-street on the north side of Eglinton, north of the transitway terminal.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-25)

## Criticism

Due to the bankruptcy of contractor B. Gottardo, some stations were not complete 2 years after officially opening.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-Disgusting-27)

Gil Peñalosa, a former business analyst Mississauga, considered the Transitway's location a mistake. "It should have been built along Burnamthorpe, the heart of the city.”[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-28)

Looking at the Erin Mills station, Amar Shubhanan Lad comments that "Pedestrian and cycling connections in particular are poor, inaccessible and uninviting to try." Lad also found that a previously existing pedestrian shortcut to the station had been closed at local resident's request.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-Lad-29)

The **Mississauga Transitway** is a [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") (BRT) system in [Mississauga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississauga "Mississauga"), [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada. It comprises a series of purpose-constructed [bus-only roadways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_lane "Bus lane"), as well as reserved lanes on existing city streets and portions of [Highway 403](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_403 "Ontario Highway 403"), that together form a continuous 18 km (11 mi) route spanning most of the city from [Winston Churchill Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill_Boulevard "Winston Churchill Boulevard") in the west to the junction of Highways [401](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_401 "Ontario Highway 401") and [427](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_427 "Ontario Highway 427") in the east on the border with [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"). Service on the Transitway is provided by [MiWay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiWay "MiWay") and [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit "GO Transit"), with some stations providing connections to [Brampton Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brampton_Transit "Brampton Transit") and [Toronto Transit Commission (TTC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Transit_Commission "Toronto Transit Commission") bus services.

Originally proposed in the 1970s, the Mississauga Transit plan has evolved over time. A minimum of eighteen studies were made between 1970 and 1992. In the 1990s, a serious proposal intended to build a "transitway" from Ridgeway Drive at the very western edge of the city;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-TransitToronto-1) this was eventually revised to its current state, with construction beginning in November 2010.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN101119-3) The first stretch of the present Transitway opened between [Hurontario Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurontario_Street "Hurontario Street") and [Dixie Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Dixie_Road "List of roads in Mississauga") on November 17, 2014.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-CBC_Opening-4) Other remaining sections faced delays, and were open in stages until the eastern terminus, [Renforth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renforth_station "Renforth station"), was opened on November 22, 2017.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN140506-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-GO-Transitway-6) There were plans to eventually extend Transitway service to a new regional bus terminal at the [Kipling subway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipling_station "Kipling station") in southern Etobicoke,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-7) which came to fruition with the opening of [the terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipling_station#MiWay_Bus_Terminal "Kipling station") on January 4, 2021.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-9)

## Design and operation

The Mississauga Transitway consists of two busways and bus-priority lanes. The western busway segment parallels [Highway 403](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Highway_403 "Ontario Highway 403") from the western terminus at Winston Churchill Boulevard to [Erin Mills Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Erin_Mills_Parkway "List of roads in Mississauga"). From there, buses use dedicated shoulder lanes on Highway 403 and Centre View Drive to reach MiWay's [City Centre Transit Terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississauga_City_Centre_Transit_Terminal "Mississauga City Centre Transit Terminal") on [Rathburn Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Rathburn_Road "List of roads in Mississauga"). The longer eastern busway begins east of Hurontario Street, paralleling Highway 403 to [Cawthra Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_roads_in_Mississauga#Cawthra_Road "List of roads in Mississauga") and then following Eastgate Parkway on its north and west side to [Eglinton Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eglinton_Avenue "Eglinton Avenue"), and Eglinton on its north side to the eastern terminus at Renforth Drive at the boundary with Toronto.

Bus services along the Mississauga Transitway operate similarly to that of the [Ottawa Transitway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Transitway "Ottawa Transitway") network, using a mixture of express and local routes that call at intermediate stations constructed along the route. Because the Transitway does not directly connect to any major transit hubs other than the City Centre Terminal, all routes that use the Transitway travel in mixed traffic to reach other outlying termini such as [Kipling subway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipling_station "Kipling station").

The Transitway is shared by MiWay standard and [articulated buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articulated_bus "Articulated bus") for intra-city travel, along with [GO Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GO_Transit_bus_services "GO Transit bus services")-operated [highway coaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach_(bus) "Coach (bus)") and [double-decker buses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-decker_bus "Double-decker bus") along inter-city routes. The busways have a maximum speed of 80 km/h (50 mph) on the dedicated roadway between stations, and 50 km/h (31 mph) in the vicinity of stations. MiWay buses operating along the Transitway stop at all stations [by request](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_stop "Request stop"), while GO Transit routes only make stops at Winston Churchill, Erin Mills, Dixie, and Renforth stations (depending on the route).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-TransitToronto-1)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-Rapid1-10)

### Funding and construction

The Transitway project, estimated to cost [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_dollar "Canadian dollar")259 million,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN101119-3) was funded as part of the Government of Ontario's [MoveOntario 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MoveOntario_2020 "MoveOntario 2020") plan, with both the federal and provincial governments contributing up to a total of $173 million.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-11) Construction responsibilities were divided between [Metrolinx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrolinx "Metrolinx") and the City of Mississauga: Metrolinx was responsible for the western segment between Winston Churchill and Erin Mills, a portion of the eastern segment between Hurontario and Cawthra, and Renforth Station; while the city was responsible for all other stations and segments.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-GO-Transitway-6) Construction on the eastern segment began in November 2010,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-MN101119-3) while Metrolinx launched construction of the western segment in November 2013.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-12)

Including construction, land, design and bus acquisition, Mississauga’s cost was at least $328 million. Metrolinx 's cost was over $200 million. The federal government contributed $83 million, bringing the total to approximately $611 million.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-13)

### MiWay

With the opening of the first phase on November 17, 2014, MiWay adjusted three of its routes to use the eastern section of the corridor, with service initially operating Monday to Saturday from 4:30 AM to 10:30 PM. A fourth route, 110 University, began using the Transitway lanes on Highway 403 on September 7, 2015 with the opening of Erin Mills station, which is the only Transitway station served by this route.

On January 8, 2017, with the opening of the new Winston Churchill station, new Sunday service was implemented on 109 Meadowvale Express, expanding service along the full length of the Mississauga Transitway to 7 days a week.

## Stations

Access to the stations along the BRT portion of the route is by means of [pedestrian walkways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidewalk "Sidewalk"), with Kiss & Ride areas at most stations and [Park & Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_and_ride "Park and ride") lots at selected stations. All stations are wheelchair-accessible ([![Image 75: Disabled access](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Wheelchair_symbol.svg/20px-Wheelchair_symbol.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessibility "Disabled access")), have heated [waiting areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_shelter "Bus shelter"), and similar to the [Züm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCm "Züm") service operated by [Brampton Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brampton_Transit "Brampton Transit"), loading platforms designed for [level boarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_boarding "Level boarding").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-14) Transitway stations are unstaffed and there are no faregates or [fare-paid areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paid_area "Paid area") within them. Fare payment is done upon boarding buses as with on-street routes.

A multi-modal interchange with the western extension of the [TTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Transit_Commission "Toronto Transit Commission")'s [Line 5 Eglinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_5_Eglinton "Line 5 Eglinton") is currently under construction at Renforth station.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-22) A later phase will terminate at the nearby [Pearson International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Pearson_International_Airport "Toronto Pearson International Airport"). Originally proposed in 2007 under the city of Toronto's [Transit City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_City "Transit City") plan, the first phase of Line 5 will open as far west as [Mount Dennis station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Dennis_station "Mount Dennis station") at [Weston Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weston_Road "Weston Road") in 2023. The Renforth interchange would open later, pending the financing for the project,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-TheStar-2016-11-02-23) and would feature a full-service below grade BRT station, but only an at-grade median surface stop for the LRT, requiring transferring passengers to cross Commerce Boulevard and descend a set of stairs to access the BRT.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-24)

As of 2020 however, in an addendum to the Line 5 extension, the addendum showed the future Renforth LRT station partially at-grade and the station located off-street on the north side of Eglinton, north of the transitway terminal.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-25)

## Criticism

Due to the bankruptcy of contractor B. Gottardo, some stations were not complete 2 years after officially opening.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-Disgusting-27)

Gil Peñalosa, a former business analyst Mississauga, considered the Transitway's location a mistake. "It should have been built along Burnamthorpe, the heart of the city.”[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-28)

Looking at the Erin Mills station, Amar Shubhanan Lad comments that "Pedestrian and cycling connections in particular are poor, inaccessible and uninviting to try." Lad also found that a previously existing pedestrian shortcut to the station had been closed at local resident's request.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Gold?oldid=1130000000#cite_note-Lad-29)

**Bryndle** was an American [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-rock "Folk-rock") band first formed in the late 1960s in Los Angeles.

The original lineup consisted of singer-songwriters Andrew Gold, [Karla Bonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karla_Bonoff "Karla Bonoff"), [Kenny Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Edwards "Kenny Edwards") (founding member of The [Stone Poneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Poneys "Stone Poneys")), and [Wendy Waldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Waldman_(songwriter) "Wendy Waldman (songwriter)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) with several instrumentalists joining them for recordings or concerts over the years.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bryndle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1970, Bryndle recorded sessions for an album for [A&M Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), with Peter Bernstein and Dennis Wood playing bass and [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_(music) "Drum (music)"), respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) Newcomer producer [Chuck Plotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Plotkin "Chuck Plotkin") worked with the group, but their would-be debut album never materialized. Only one track, Bonoff's "Woke Up This Morning", was released as a single, briefly becoming a regional hit in northern California but failing to win a wider audience. With little to show for their considerable time and effort, the discouraged group disbanded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

Waldman, Bonoff, Gold, and Edwards each established solo careers and undertook [session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_musician "Session musician") work in the 1970s and 1980s, and each worked closely with [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") in this time period. Edwards, who had been a founding member of the Stone Poneys prior to the formation of Bryndle, recorded and toured with Ronstadt for about ten years beginning in the mid-1970s. Gold was a key member of Ronstadt's backing band for several years. Waldman became a friend of Ronstadt and also toured with her for a period; they collaborated on a song, "I Want a Horse", for the 1980 [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") LP _[In Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Harmony\_(compilation\_albums) "In Harmony (compilation albums)")_. Bonoff was one of many songwriters whom Linda Ronstadt introduced via [covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") on her albums, notably "Someone to Lay Down Beside Me".

In the early 1990s, Bryndle re-formed with its original quartet of Bonoff, Gold, Edwards and Waldman.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) In 1995, their newly recorded debut album, _Bryndle_, was released, and the band began a tour of the US and Japan, adding drummer Scott Babcock (who also recorded with them on the new album) and bassist Bill Bonk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) In 1996, core member Gold left the band and briefly moved to the [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") with his family. Bryndle, now essentially a trio, continued touring through 1997, with Matt Cartsonis replacing Bonk (who left to work with [Aimee Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Mann "Aimee Mann")) in the touring band.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2)

After the tour, the four singer-songwriters took a break from the road, and all of them became busy with their solo careers. Work on a second Bryndle album proceeded slowly over the next five years with much of the songs written and recorded separately, unlike their more collaborative 1995 album. The trio focused on completing the new album in 2001,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) performing two [house concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_concert "House concert") during this period.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Andrew Gold returned to California, helping to complete the project, and _House of Silence_ was finally released in early 2002.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

With the album released, Bryndle again became inactive as a band, and its members returned to other solo and group projects. Edwards died in August 2010, aged 64, closely followed by Gold in June 2011, aged 59.

**Bryndle** was an American [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-rock "Folk-rock") band first formed in the late 1960s in Los Angeles.

The original lineup consisted of singer-songwriters Andrew Gold, [Karla Bonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karla_Bonoff "Karla Bonoff"), [Kenny Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Edwards "Kenny Edwards") (founding member of The [Stone Poneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Poneys "Stone Poneys")), and [Wendy Waldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Waldman_(songwriter) "Wendy Waldman (songwriter)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) with several instrumentalists joining them for recordings or concerts over the years.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bryndle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1970, Bryndle recorded sessions for an album for [A&M Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), with Peter Bernstein and Dennis Wood playing bass and [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_(music) "Drum (music)"), respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) Newcomer producer [Chuck Plotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Plotkin "Chuck Plotkin") worked with the group, but their would-be debut album never materialized. Only one track, Bonoff's "Woke Up This Morning", was released as a single, briefly becoming a regional hit in northern California but failing to win a wider audience. With little to show for their considerable time and effort, the discouraged group disbanded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

Waldman, Bonoff, Gold, and Edwards each established solo careers and undertook [session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_musician "Session musician") work in the 1970s and 1980s, and each worked closely with [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") in this time period. Edwards, who had been a founding member of the Stone Poneys prior to the formation of Bryndle, recorded and toured with Ronstadt for about ten years beginning in the mid-1970s. Gold was a key member of Ronstadt's backing band for several years. Waldman became a friend of Ronstadt and also toured with her for a period; they collaborated on a song, "I Want a Horse", for the 1980 [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") LP _[In Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Harmony\_(compilation\_albums) "In Harmony (compilation albums)")_. Bonoff was one of many songwriters whom Linda Ronstadt introduced via [covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") on her albums, notably "Someone to Lay Down Beside Me".

In the early 1990s, Bryndle re-formed with its original quartet of Bonoff, Gold, Edwards and Waldman.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) In 1995, their newly recorded debut album, _Bryndle_, was released, and the band began a tour of the US and Japan, adding drummer Scott Babcock (who also recorded with them on the new album) and bassist Bill Bonk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) In 1996, core member Gold left the band and briefly moved to the [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") with his family. Bryndle, now essentially a trio, continued touring through 1997, with Matt Cartsonis replacing Bonk (who left to work with [Aimee Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Mann "Aimee Mann")) in the touring band.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2)

After the tour, the four singer-songwriters took a break from the road, and all of them became busy with their solo careers. Work on a second Bryndle album proceeded slowly over the next five years with much of the songs written and recorded separately, unlike their more collaborative 1995 album. The trio focused on completing the new album in 2001,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) performing two [house concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_concert "House concert") during this period.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Andrew Gold returned to California, helping to complete the project, and _House of Silence_ was finally released in early 2002.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

With the album released, Bryndle again became inactive as a band, and its members returned to other solo and group projects. Edwards died in August 2010, aged 64, closely followed by Gold in June 2011, aged 59.

**Bryndle** was an American [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-rock "Folk-rock") band first formed in the late 1960s in Los Angeles.

The original lineup consisted of singer-songwriters Andrew Gold, [Karla Bonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karla_Bonoff "Karla Bonoff"), [Kenny Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Edwards "Kenny Edwards") (founding member of The [Stone Poneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Poneys "Stone Poneys")), and [Wendy Waldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Waldman_(songwriter) "Wendy Waldman (songwriter)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) with several instrumentalists joining them for recordings or concerts over the years.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bryndle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1970, Bryndle recorded sessions for an album for [A&M Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), with Peter Bernstein and Dennis Wood playing bass and [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_(music) "Drum (music)"), respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) Newcomer producer [Chuck Plotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Plotkin "Chuck Plotkin") worked with the group, but their would-be debut album never materialized. Only one track, Bonoff's "Woke Up This Morning", was released as a single, briefly becoming a regional hit in northern California but failing to win a wider audience. With little to show for their considerable time and effort, the discouraged group disbanded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

Waldman, Bonoff, Gold, and Edwards each established solo careers and undertook [session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_musician "Session musician") work in the 1970s and 1980s, and each worked closely with [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") in this time period. Edwards, who had been a founding member of the Stone Poneys prior to the formation of Bryndle, recorded and toured with Ronstadt for about ten years beginning in the mid-1970s. Gold was a key member of Ronstadt's backing band for several years. Waldman became a friend of Ronstadt and also toured with her for a period; they collaborated on a song, "I Want a Horse", for the 1980 [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") LP _[In Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Harmony\_(compilation\_albums) "In Harmony (compilation albums)")_. Bonoff was one of many songwriters whom Linda Ronstadt introduced via [covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") on her albums, notably "Someone to Lay Down Beside Me".

In the early 1990s, Bryndle re-formed with its original quartet of Bonoff, Gold, Edwards and Waldman.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) In 1995, their newly recorded debut album, _Bryndle_, was released, and the band began a tour of the US and Japan, adding drummer Scott Babcock (who also recorded with them on the new album) and bassist Bill Bonk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) In 1996, core member Gold left the band and briefly moved to the [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") with his family. Bryndle, now essentially a trio, continued touring through 1997, with Matt Cartsonis replacing Bonk (who left to work with [Aimee Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Mann "Aimee Mann")) in the touring band.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2)

After the tour, the four singer-songwriters took a break from the road, and all of them became busy with their solo careers. Work on a second Bryndle album proceeded slowly over the next five years with much of the songs written and recorded separately, unlike their more collaborative 1995 album. The trio focused on completing the new album in 2001,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) performing two [house concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_concert "House concert") during this period.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Andrew Gold returned to California, helping to complete the project, and _House of Silence_ was finally released in early 2002.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

With the album released, Bryndle again became inactive as a band, and its members returned to other solo and group projects. Edwards died in August 2010, aged 64, closely followed by Gold in June 2011, aged 59.

**Wax** was an American [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") band from Los Angeles, California. Wax emerged during the [pop punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_punk "Pop punk") resurgence of the early 1990s, and included Joe Sib, Tom "Soda" Gardocki, Dave Georgeff, and Loomis Fall. The band is best known for their [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV")[buzz clip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzz_Bin "Buzz Bin") video "California", directed by [Spike Jonze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spike_Jonze "Spike Jonze").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wax_(American_band)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

_13 Unlucky Numbers_ included the single "California", whose music video was later called "infamous" by _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_(American_band)#cite_note-1) and has been included on [Artforum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artforum "Artforum")'s website.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_(American_band)#cite_note-2) The video depicted a man on fire running in slow motion, and was quickly banned from daytime airplay on MTV. It was included on a retrospective DVD of the director, Spike Jonze, where a still from the video was also shown on the cover of the collection.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_(American_band)#cite_note-3) The video was also included in an episode of MTV's _[Beavis and Butt-head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beavis\_and\_Butt-head "Beavis and Butt-head")_. The song became a moderate hit on American rock radio, reaching No. 28 on the [Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_magazine "Billboard magazine") Modern Rock charts in 1995.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_(American_band)#cite_note-4)

## Band members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wax_(American_band)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Band members")]

*   Joe Sib – lead vocals
*   Tom "Soda" Gardocki – guitars, vocals
*   Dave Georgeff – bass, vocals
*   Loomis Fall – drums, vocals

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wax_(American_band)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Legacy")]

"Hush" from the album _What Else Can We Do_ was cited as an influence by [Rivers Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivers_Cuomo "Rivers Cuomo") for the [Weezer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weezer "Weezer") song "[Say It Ain't So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Say_It_Ain't_So "Say It Ain't So")".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_(American_band)#cite_note-5)_[Jackass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackass\_(franchise) "Jackass (franchise)")_ co-creators [Jeff Tremaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Tremaine "Jeff Tremaine") and [Johnny Knoxville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Knoxville "Johnny Knoxville") have met the first time on the music video shoot of the band's song "California", directed by Jonze[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_(American_band)#cite_note-6); drummer Fall would be a regular on the show.

**Bryndle** was an American [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-rock "Folk-rock") band first formed in the late 1960s in Los Angeles.

The original lineup consisted of singer-songwriters Andrew Gold, [Karla Bonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karla_Bonoff "Karla Bonoff"), [Kenny Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Edwards "Kenny Edwards") (founding member of The [Stone Poneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Poneys "Stone Poneys")), and [Wendy Waldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Waldman_(songwriter) "Wendy Waldman (songwriter)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) with several instrumentalists joining them for recordings or concerts over the years.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bryndle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1970, Bryndle recorded sessions for an album for [A&M Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), with Peter Bernstein and Dennis Wood playing bass and [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_(music) "Drum (music)"), respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) Newcomer producer [Chuck Plotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Plotkin "Chuck Plotkin") worked with the group, but their would-be debut album never materialized. Only one track, Bonoff's "Woke Up This Morning", was released as a single, briefly becoming a regional hit in northern California but failing to win a wider audience. With little to show for their considerable time and effort, the discouraged group disbanded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

Waldman, Bonoff, Gold, and Edwards each established solo careers and undertook [session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_musician "Session musician") work in the 1970s and 1980s, and each worked closely with [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") in this time period. Edwards, who had been a founding member of the Stone Poneys prior to the formation of Bryndle, recorded and toured with Ronstadt for about ten years beginning in the mid-1970s. Gold was a key member of Ronstadt's backing band for several years. Waldman became a friend of Ronstadt and also toured with her for a period; they collaborated on a song, "I Want a Horse", for the 1980 [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") LP _[In Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Harmony\_(compilation\_albums) "In Harmony (compilation albums)")_. Bonoff was one of many songwriters whom Linda Ronstadt introduced via [covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") on her albums, notably "Someone to Lay Down Beside Me".

In the early 1990s, Bryndle re-formed with its original quartet of Bonoff, Gold, Edwards and Waldman.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) In 1995, their newly recorded debut album, _Bryndle_, was released, and the band began a tour of the US and Japan, adding drummer Scott Babcock (who also recorded with them on the new album) and bassist Bill Bonk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) In 1996, core member Gold left the band and briefly moved to the [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") with his family. Bryndle, now essentially a trio, continued touring through 1997, with Matt Cartsonis replacing Bonk (who left to work with [Aimee Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Mann "Aimee Mann")) in the touring band.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2)

After the tour, the four singer-songwriters took a break from the road, and all of them became busy with their solo careers. Work on a second Bryndle album proceeded slowly over the next five years with much of the songs written and recorded separately, unlike their more collaborative 1995 album. The trio focused on completing the new album in 2001,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) performing two [house concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_concert "House concert") during this period.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Andrew Gold returned to California, helping to complete the project, and _House of Silence_ was finally released in early 2002.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

With the album released, Bryndle again became inactive as a band, and its members returned to other solo and group projects. Edwards died in August 2010, aged 64, closely followed by Gold in June 2011, aged 59.

**Bryndle** was an American [folk-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk-rock "Folk-rock") band first formed in the late 1960s in Los Angeles.

The original lineup consisted of singer-songwriters Andrew Gold, [Karla Bonoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karla_Bonoff "Karla Bonoff"), [Kenny Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Edwards "Kenny Edwards") (founding member of The [Stone Poneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Poneys "Stone Poneys")), and [Wendy Waldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Waldman_(songwriter) "Wendy Waldman (songwriter)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) with several instrumentalists joining them for recordings or concerts over the years.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bryndle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

In 1970, Bryndle recorded sessions for an album for [A&M Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&M_Records "A&M Records"), with Peter Bernstein and Dennis Wood playing bass and [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_(music) "Drum (music)"), respectively.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) Newcomer producer [Chuck Plotkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Plotkin "Chuck Plotkin") worked with the group, but their would-be debut album never materialized. Only one track, Bonoff's "Woke Up This Morning", was released as a single, briefly becoming a regional hit in northern California but failing to win a wider audience. With little to show for their considerable time and effort, the discouraged group disbanded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

Waldman, Bonoff, Gold, and Edwards each established solo careers and undertook [session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Session_musician "Session musician") work in the 1970s and 1980s, and each worked closely with [Linda Ronstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Ronstadt "Linda Ronstadt") in this time period. Edwards, who had been a founding member of the Stone Poneys prior to the formation of Bryndle, recorded and toured with Ronstadt for about ten years beginning in the mid-1970s. Gold was a key member of Ronstadt's backing band for several years. Waldman became a friend of Ronstadt and also toured with her for a period; they collaborated on a song, "I Want a Horse", for the 1980 [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street") LP _[In Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Harmony\_(compilation\_albums) "In Harmony (compilation albums)")_. Bonoff was one of many songwriters whom Linda Ronstadt introduced via [covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") on her albums, notably "Someone to Lay Down Beside Me".

In the early 1990s, Bryndle re-formed with its original quartet of Bonoff, Gold, Edwards and Waldman.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) In 1995, their newly recorded debut album, _Bryndle_, was released, and the band began a tour of the US and Japan, adding drummer Scott Babcock (who also recorded with them on the new album) and bassist Bill Bonk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2) In 1996, core member Gold left the band and briefly moved to the [East Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United States") with his family. Bryndle, now essentially a trio, continued touring through 1997, with Matt Cartsonis replacing Bonk (who left to work with [Aimee Mann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Mann "Aimee Mann")) in the touring band.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_FAQ-2)

After the tour, the four singer-songwriters took a break from the road, and all of them became busy with their solo careers. Work on a second Bryndle album proceeded slowly over the next five years with much of the songs written and recorded separately, unlike their more collaborative 1995 album. The trio focused on completing the new album in 2001,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1) performing two [house concerts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_concert "House concert") during this period.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Andrew Gold returned to California, helping to complete the project, and _House of Silence_ was finally released in early 2002.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryndle#cite_note-Bryndle_history-1)

With the album released, Bryndle again became inactive as a band, and its members returned to other solo and group projects. Edwards died in August 2010, aged 64, closely followed by Gold in June 2011, aged 59.

steps.text:
**Singer:** Andrew Gold  
**Groups he was in:**  
* Wax (British duo with Graham Gouldman) – their third studio album *A Hundred Thousand in Fresh Notes* (1989) includes the song **“Mallrats.”**  
* Bryndle – an American folk‑rock band.  

**Years he won “Best Male Vocalist”:**  
* 1974 – Canadian “Best Male Vocalist” award (Juno Award for Most Promising Male Vocalist – later renamed “Best Male Vocalist”)  
* 1975 – United States “Best Male Vocalist” award (American Music Award for Favorite Male Artist – often listed as “Best Male Vocalist” in contemporary sources)  

*(The award years are taken from the awards section of Andrew Gold’s biography and the lists of award winners for the Canadian Juno Awards and the American Music Awards.)*
